newsitem.title: USA: Ex-brokers charged in Escambia Cty, Fla.investments.
newsitem.headline: Ex-brokers charged in Escambia Cty, Fla.investments.

text.p: Four brokers formerly with the Houston office of First Montauk Securities Corp were charged with racketeering Wednesday in connection with the sale of derivative securities to the comptroller for Escambia County, Fla.

Escambia County prosecutors charged that Kent Tippets Black, Joel Lee Hurst, David Eric Lynch and Larry Eugene Muller engaged in a scheme to allegedly defraud former Comptroller Joseph Flowers by manipulating the prices of unsuitably risky securities that cost Escambia taxpayers about $15 million dollars.
If convicted of the charge they would face up to 30 years in prison and fines three times the county's losses.
None of the defendants were in custody Wednesday, an aide to Assistant State Attorney Russell Edgar said. They could not be reached for comment.
First Montauk's general counsel, Robert Rabinowitz, said the four were dismissed from the firm due to market conditions before the firm learned of the allegations about their trades.
"The firm in New Jersey and the principals of the firm had absolutely no knowledge of these transactions," Rabinowitz said.

First Montauk is headquartered in Red Bank, N.J., and was not charged in the criminal case. The company agreed in March to pay the county $900,000 to settle a civil lawsuit filed against it by Escambia County.

Joanne Kraynak, an investigator with the Florida comptroller's office, said in an affidavit supporting the charges that the brokers allegedly misrepresented the value and suitability of the securities and manipulated the prices.
"These securities were highly volatile and had substantial market and liquidity risks," Kraynak said in the affidavit.

The securities were bought with tax revneues needed for short-term expenses. As a result the county was forced to sell them at tremendous losses, and in some instances, to borrow money to pay its costs.
The affidavit said Black sold the county more than $27 million of derivatives over four years, earning more than $300,000 in commissions from the county.

It said he allegedly induced Flowers to buy them by telling him First Montauk would buy them back at higher prices in 30 to 60 days, "essentially guaranteeing the former comptroller profits in volatile, risky issues."
Kraynak said the brokers bought all or most of the tranches for some derivative issues, enabling them to control the issues and manipulate the prices.
She said the brokers also allegedly engaged in a "round robin" trading scheme that allowed them to mark up the securities' prices by as much as 16 percent.

Typically, Hurst, Lynch or Muller would allegedly call another dealer and enlist him as a "straw buyer" to purchase, hold and re-sell the security at an agreed price for a small fee, the affidavit said.
After repurchasing the securities from the straw buyers, First Montauk would then sell them to Escambia or other customers, the affidavit alleged.

"The county and other customers who paid excessive prices for the issues did not know that the issues they bought had been traded two, three or even four times by First Montauk after they (the county) had committed to buy them at specific set prices," Kraynak said.
The documents said other customers besides the county also suffered "substantial market losses" but did not identify them.
Escambia County invested $45 million in derivative securities, including inverse floaters and collateralized mortgage obligations, between 1990 and 1994.
When interest rates rose in late 1994, the portfolio lost half its value. The market eventually turned and the securities were sold last year at a loss of about $15 million.

Flowers later pleaded no contest to four misdemeanor charges that he mismanaged taxpayer money by investing in unsuitably risky securities and illegally entering into a computer lease-purchase agreement.
--Jane Sutton, 305-374-5013
